classification.reasoning: Purpose: The crate is `openssl-sys`, a very well-known, foundational crate providing FFI bindings to OpenSSL, with massive download volume (over 468 million downloads) and a long history on crates.io (over 11 years old). Sources: The build script reads standard environment variables (`TARGET`, `DEP_BSSL_CONF`) and invokes standard build tools like `pkg-config` and `bindgen` via `Command::new`, which is standard and expected for a native OpenSSL binding crate. Sinks: Unsafe blocks and `extern "C"` FFI declarations are used exclusively for interacting with the native C OpenSSL library (e.g., cryptographic key structures and functions such as `AES_set_encrypt_key`), which is the core purpose of a `-sys` FFI crate. Flow: Native FFI calls without malicious data exfiltration. Anomalies: None. The raw matches for `process_spawn` (`pkg-config`, `bindgen`) and `env_var_read` are entirely benign and expected for a complex native dependency build script, aligning with pattern-benign-false-positive-build-rs. Conclusion: The crate is completely legitimate.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: legitimate build.rs signals that are NOT malicious
retrieved_context.text: Common benign reasons a crate's build.rs may trigger a raw signal match: checking the installed rustc/cargo version via Command::new (used by serde and many other major crates to gate feature availability); generating code from a schema or protobuf definition, sometimes fetched over network from a first-party, well-known source; reading a small number of standard, non-sensitive environment variables like OUT_DIR, TARGET, or CARGO_PKG_VERSION which Cargo itself sets. A high-quality classifier should not flag these alone -- context (destination of network calls, sensitivity of specific env var names read, and the crate's stated purpose) matters more than raw signal presence.
retrieved_context.source: synthesized from observed benign build.rs behavior, e.g. serde

retrieved_context.title: logs-update: credential and file stealer in library code, no build script (September 2026)
retrieved_context.text: A crate published on 2026-09-10 that presents itself as a terminal progress-bar library but renders nothing. It has NO build script, so it does not run during `cargo build` of a dependent; it runs when its binary is executed (for example after `cargo install`) or when a dependent calls its run() function. It POSTs a machine fingerprint (username, OS, local IP) to an attacker web endpoint; reads the project's .env and trading-bot config files and POSTs them; walks the filesystem and POSTs the contents of .env, .json, .txt, .doc/.docx and .xlsx files; and on Linux appends an attacker's SSH public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for remote login. It targets crypto trading-bot developers. Reported as malicious in every version. Lesson: a build-script-only detector sees nothing here; the tell-tale combination is network POSTs plus filesystem walking plus credential-file paths in library code.

retrieved_context.title: arrayref / internment / append-only-vec trojanized via a malicious dependency (August 2026)
retrieved_context.text: On 2026-08-20, arrayref 0.3.10, internment 0.8.7 and append-only-vec 0.1.9 were published to crates.io from a maintainer account that appears to have been compromised. For arrayref the source was unchanged genuine code; the release added a dependency on the malicious crate proc-macro1. proc-macro1 typosquats proc-macro2 (its library source is a copy, so dependent builds succeed) and forges the real author's name in its metadata; its build.rs reconstructs a base64-encoded URL, downloads an architecture-specific remote binary over TLS with certificate validation disabled, and runs it detached with a command-and-control address as argument, unconditionally on every supported-platform build. internment and append-only-vec added a dependency on an attacker-controlled crate with the same kind of build-script payload. Further crates (aovine, arone, aronenao, proc-macro-en, tinymember) belong to the same campaign; their build scripts were attributed from the campaign rather than analyzed individually. Earlier releases of the trojanized crates are reported as unaffected, and the malicious releases were removed. Lesson: the trojanized crate's own code can be clean; the signal is a NEW dependency whose build script downloads and executes a remote binary.
